- If we have a monthly commit, how are rounding/minimums applied for these bursts? Example invoice line would help.
- Any recommended packaging to avoid one-off huge spikes blowing out unit economics?

We need to size a PO and want to understand the worst-case and recommended mitigation (e.g., commit tiers, session buckets, or reserved capacity).

Hi Tom,

Thanks for the clear note. Short answer: we bill per-token but we provide two pricing/packaging patterns to help smooth spikes. I'll outline both and attach a simple workbook with sample invoices.

Options we recommend:

1) Per-call (raw) billing — simplest
- Every request is tokenized and billed at per-token rates.
- Rounding: we round billed tokens up to the nearest 100-token quantum for short calls, and up to the nearest 1,000-token quantum for long-form calls by default.
- Minimums: a per-request floor of 50 tokens applies.
- Pros: predictability per-request, no commitment.
- Cons: single huge call will show up as a large line item.

2) Bucketed/commit packaging — smoothing for spikes (recommended for you)
- Commit to a monthly token volume (e.g., 5M tokens/mo). Overuse is charged at an overage rate.
- We maintain a rolling smoothing window that allows ephemeral bursts to draw from the committed bucket before billing overage.
- Rounding is applied at the bucket level: we aggregate tokens across requests and apply a final rounding to the nearest 1,000-token billing unit when converting to invoice lines.
- Advantage: sporadic 100k requests are amortized across the month instead of appearing as a single big charge.

Quick example (see attached spreadsheet for more):
- Month commit: 5,000,000 tokens
- Bursts: 3 calls @ 100,000 tokens = 300,000 tokens (1)
- Bulk of calls: 4,700,000 tokens
- Total usage: 5,000,000 tokens -> billed at committed rates.

(1) If you were on raw billing, those same three calls would be rounded individually to 1,000-token quanta and billed at on-demand rates.

Pilot offer: to make the transition easier, we typically offer a temporary smoothing concession for the first 60 days of a commit: we apply a 20% discount on any overage rate for the first two months and we prorate the commit mid-month if you sign a PO mid-cycle.

Tom — hi, Karthik here (pricing). Below are two concise worked examples using your 100k bursts so you can see invoice-level mechanics. I've attached a sample invoice text file for the on-demand scenario.

Assumptions:
- On-demand rate: $0.00012 / token
- Committed rate (5M/mo): $0.00009 / token
- Rounding quanta: short calls -> 100 tokens (round up), long calls -> 1,000 tokens (round up)
- Per-call floor: 50 tokens

Scenario A — On-demand billing (no commit)
- 3 long calls, raw tokens: 100,000 each -> rounding -> 100,000 (no extra since already multiple of 1,000)
- Billed tokens for those calls: 300,000 tokens @ $0.00012 = $36.00
- Many short calls (~100 tokens each) aggregated to 20,000 tokens -> billed at rounding quanta -> 20,000 tokens @ $0.00012 = $2.40
- Invoice total sample line items:
  * Chat short calls (20k tokens): $2.40
  * Long-form calls (3x100k): $36.00
  * Total: $38.40

Scenario B — 5M commit (recommended)
- Commit: 5,000,000 tokens @ $0.00009 = $450.00/month (pre-tax)
- Usage example: 5,000,000 tokens total -> no overage
- If mid-month you sign and the commit is prorated: we compute a prorated commit amount (calendar prorate) and the remaining days are billed at on-demand rates or credited against the prorated commit per SOW.

Rounding/aggregation note:
- With the commit, we aggregate usage and then apply a single rounding step when materializing invoice lines (nearest 1,000-token unit). This prevents isolated rounding inflation that you'd see on per-call billing.

Discount proposal for Acme Retail (commercial):
- 6-month minimum commit: 5M tokens/mo -> 10% off committed rate for the length of the term
- First 60 days: overage charged at 50% of standard overage rate (grace period to absorb tail risk)
- Mid-month PoS signing: calendar-day prorate of commit with overage protection as described above

If that commercial structure looks acceptable I can get Legal to draft a short SOW and we can include explicit examples for proration and rounding in the appendix.

Attached: sample-invoice-acme.txt (plain text) — shows how lines would appear for on-demand vs commit.

Thanks — happy to model a few different commit sizes if you share a sample day.

—Karthik
